nameStory: Prairie Coreopsis gets its "prairie" name from its natural home in the grasslands of central North America, where it thrives in open, sunny spaces. The "coreopsis" part comes from Greek words meaning "bug-like," referring to the shape of its seeds that reminded early botanists of tiny insects. Its alternate name "tickseed" also hints at these small, dark seeds that look like little ticks!
description: Prairie Coreopsis is a cheerful wildflower that brings bright yellow, daisy-like blooms to sunny spots from summer into fall. This sturdy perennial grows 1-3 feet tall with distinctive deeply-lobed leaves that look almost like fingers reaching out from the stem. While common in Midwest prairies, it's quite rare in New England, making any sighting here a special treat. The plant forms small colonies through underground stems, creating patches of golden flowers that attract butterflies and other pollinators.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: The most distinctive feature - deeply divided leaves that look like spread fingers or a bird's foot, with 3-5 narrow, pointed lobes radiating from a central point. Feel the leaves and you'll notice they're somewhat thick and sturdy with a slightly rough texture.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright golden-yellow flowers about 1-2 inches across with 8 broad petals that have 3-4 small notches at their tips, giving them a ragged edge. The center is darker yellow and feels slightly bumpy to the touch.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms upright clumps 1-3 feet tall with multiple branching stems that feel firm and slightly ridged. Plants often grow in small colonies, spreading slowly by underground runners.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Small, dark, oval seeds that are flat and thin like tiny watermelon seeds, often with small bristles or wings. They feel papery and are easily carried by wind.

habitat: In New England, Prairie Coreopsis is extremely rare and typically found only in sunny, well-drained locations like old fields, prairie restorations, or naturalized garden areas where it may have been planted. It prefers open grasslands and meadows with full sun exposure. Given its rarity here (only one recorded observation), any sighting would likely be in a deliberately planted prairie garden or restoration site rather than a truly wild population.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as small rosettes of the characteristic fingered leaves, which are easier to spot before surrounding vegetation gets tall.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with bright yellow flowers appearing from mid to late summer, making identification straightforward when flowers are present.
seasonality.fall: Flowers may continue into early fall, followed by seed heads that turn brown and papery, releasing small dark seeds that scatter in the wind.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level, leaving only dried stems and seed heads that may persist, making winter identification nearly impossible.

funFact: This prairie native can survive fires that would kill most other plants - in fact, it actually benefits from occasional burning, which clears competing vegetation and stimulates new growth from its deep underground stems, just like it evolved to do in natural grassland fires!
confusionNotes: The deeply divided, finger-like leaves make Prairie Coreopsis quite distinctive among the coreopsis family, but it could be confused with other yellow composite flowers when not in bloom. However, no other coreopsis in New England has leaves divided into such narrow, finger-like segments - most have simple, undivided leaves or leaves with just a few broad lobes.
contextualKnowledge: Prairie Coreopsis is far outside its natural range in New England - it's primarily a Midwest prairie species. Any plants found here are likely garden escapes or deliberately planted in prairie restoration projects, making it more of a curiosity than a true wild New England native.
compareHints: Unlike its New England relatives like Lance-leaved Coreopsis (which has simple, narrow leaves) or Rose Coreopsis (which has thin, needle-like leaves), Prairie Coreopsis has those distinctive deeply-divided, finger-like leaves that make it unmistakable. While Whorled Coreopsis also has divided leaves, they're arranged in whorls around the stem rather than alternately like Prairie Coreopsis.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Rose Coreopsis is the only tickseed in New England with pink or white petals - all its relatives like Lance-leaved and Whorled Coreopsis have bright yellow flowers.
Among its tickseed relatives, Whorled Coreopsis is the only one with thread-like leaves arranged in distinct whorls around the stem.

Lance-leaved Coreopsis differs from other Coreopsis species by its simple, unlobed lance-shaped leaves - Rose Coreopsis has much smaller pink flowers, while Whorled Coreopsis has very finely divided, thread-like leaves.
Plains coreopsis differs from other New England coreopsis species by being an annual (dies each year) rather than perennial, and by having the most deeply divided, feathery leaves of the group.
Tall coreopsis dwarfs all other New England coreopsis species - most relatives like lance-leaved coreopsis and rose coreopsis stay under 3 feet tall.

Among New England's coreopsis species, lobed coreopsis is immediately distinguished by its uniquely shaped leaves - rose coreopsis has narrow linear leaves, lance-leaved has simple spear-shaped leaves, and whorled coreopsis has thread-like leaves in circles around the stem.

Large-flowered tickseed stands out from other New England tickseeds by its size - both the flowers and overall plant are notably larger than rose coreopsis (which has pink flowers) or lance-leaved coreopsis.
